query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Depositing a functionally graded, nanostructured protective glaze layer on the CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy surface will enable the alloy to maintain a consistently low friction coefficient and minimal wear rate across the full temperature range (25 °C to 800 °C) compared to the uncoated material.
generation.material_initial_state: Uncoated CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix which exhibits increasing wear and friction variability across the temperature range due to temperature‐dependent oxidation, phase instability, and ineffective intrinsic lubrication.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled deposition process—such as physical vapor deposition (PVD) combined with laser surface texturing—to create a functionally graded, nanostructured protective glaze layer.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests conducted from room temperature (~25 °C) to high temperature (up to 800 °C) under representative normal loads (e.g., 30 N) and sliding speeds in an oxidizing environment.
generation.structural_mediator: The engineered, graded nanolaminate glaze layer, which is designed to adapt its microstructure and composition with depth, leading to the formation of a stable, self-adaptive oxide scale during sliding.
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures, the nanostructured coating maintains high surface hardness and low shear stress, while at elevated temperatures, the designed gradient facilitates the rapid formation and retention of a robust, low-shear oxide glaze layer that minimizes adhesive, oxidative, and plastic deformation wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated CoCrFeNi alloy is expected to exhibit a uniformly low friction coefficient and significantly reduced wear rate across the full temperature range compared to the baseline uncoated material.
generation.baseline: The uncoated CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy, which shows temperature-dependent degradation in tribological performance.
generation.boundary: Performance is evaluated under sliding conditions with normal loads around 30 N and sliding speeds typical of previous studies, in an environment that becomes increasingly oxidizing with temperature, spanning from ~25 °C to 800 °C.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of glaze layer formation and its mechanical stability across the temperature gradient are not fully known, and variations in sliding speed/loading conditions may influence the coating’s self-adaptive response.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one group with the deposited graded glaze layer and one uncoated control group. Conduct sliding wear tests across the temperature range from 25 °C to 800 °C under identical loads and speeds in an oxidizing atmosphere. Use high-resolution topographical scanning and SEM/EDS analysis to monitor friction coefficients, wear rates, and the morphology of the formed surface layers.
measurements: Coefficient of friction (μ) at various temperatures
Surface morphology and oxide layer integrity via SEM
Elemental composition of worn surfaces using EDS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples fail to show a statistically significant reduction in friction coefficient and wear rate across all tested temperatures compared to the baseline uncoated alloy, or if the protective oxide glaze layer does not form and remain intact under high-temperature conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Our work uncovers a practical avenue for tailoring wear properties with multicomponent heterostructures over a wide temperature range.

For NiX, its worn track dimensions also increase at 400 °C compared to those at RT, but the worn surface remains relatively smooth and is free of debris and micro-pits (Fig. S7b). This uncovers that NiX still outperforms Ni3X in resisting the elastic–plastic deformation involved with abrasive wear even at 400 °C. The higher high-temperature hardness of NiX may be responsible for the low wear rate compared to Ni3X at 400 °C (Fig. 3A). Nanoindentation tests (Fig. S2) also show that H on the worn surface of NiX (5.9 GPa) at 400 °C is higher than that of Ni3X (4.9 GPa). In the present study, the tribological properties of different grain sizes CoCrFeMnNi HEAs were systematically analyzed based on sliding experiments and worn surface morphology characterization under different sliding speeds and normal loads. The results can be summarized as follows: Under the normal low load and low sliding speed, the main wear mechanism of FG and CG samples is adhesive wear. With the increase in sliding speed, the wear mechanisms are adhesive wear and oxidation wear. However, the material of CG is easy to soften under the action of friction heat during high sliding speed, and the oxide layer formed is easy to fracture. Under the normal high load, the wear mechanisms of FG and CG samples are mainly adhesive wear, oxidation wear, and plastic deformation with the increase of sliding speed. The oxidation layer formed on CG sample has many cracks, and the wear surface of CG sample also has plastic deformation, resulting in an increase in friction coefficient and specific wear rate and a decrease in wear resistance. Therefore, under high load and low load, FG sample has good wear resistance due to its high surface strength.

decision.trend: The research trajectory in high-entropy alloys for high‐temperature wear resistance began with modifying the bulk microstructure through powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering—in some cases adding extra elements (W in PMC8470387; Mo in PMC12655553) to induce second phases that enhance high-temperature wear resistance via lattice distortion and second‐phase strengthening. These methods have achieved improved wear performance at high temperatures through oxidation‐induced protection, but they frequently come at the expense of fluctuating friction behavior or limited effectiveness at lower temperatures. Essentially, early work addressed localized improvements (either low‐temperature friction or high‐temperature wear) by tweaking bulk composition and processing, yet a unified solution across the full temperature range remains elusive.
decision.unsolved: Maintaining consistently low friction and wear across a wide temperature span (from room temperature to 800 °C) in a CoCrFeNi matrix, without introducing multiple or competing mechanisms that are effective only in narrow regimes, continues to be a challenge.
decision.lever: Implement a controlled deposition of a functionally graded, nanostructured protective glaze layer (for example via physical vapor deposition combined with laser surface texturing) that is engineered to develop a stable, self-adaptive oxide scale during sliding across the entire temperature range.
decision.why: This approach builds on the trend of leveraging interfacial phenomena for wear reduction. Whereas prior work using compositional modifications (e.g., W, Mo alloying) improved high‐temperature performance but led to friction fluctuations or were limited to specific regimes, a strategically designed surface coating can tailor the friction interface. By engineering a gradient nanolaminate that adapts its lubrication mechanism (e.g., forming a robust yet low-shear oxide glaze) with temperature, the intervention decouples surface wear behavior from the bulk alloy properties, thus promising consistent low friction and wear across both room temperature and high-temperature (800 °C) sliding conditions. A controlled experiment comparing the friction and wear performance of the coated versus uncoated CoCrFeNi matrix over the full temperature range would provide a critical falsification test.
